etymology: Middle English bost, a loud outcry or brag, of uncertain origin. In the KJV it stands beside glory and vaunt to render Greek kauchaomai, a verb that can be holy or damning depending entirely on its object.
biblical_def: Scripture does not forbid boasting; it relocates it. The governing text sets the two ledgers side by side: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches: but let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me (Jer 9:23-24). Paul quotes the substance twice—He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord (1 Cor 1:31)—and treats boasting as the natural theological consequence of a doctrine of works. Ask where boasting went and you have asked how a man is justified: Where is boasting then? It is excluded. By what law? of works? Nay: but by the law of faith (Rom 3:27). If salvation were by works, boasting would be permitted, even appropriate. It is excluded because grace leaves nothing to bill for. James is blunter about the everyday form, the man planning his year as though tomorrow were his to spend: ye rejoice in your boastings: all such rejoicing is evil (Jas 4:16). Paul does boast—of the Corinthians, of the cross, and famously of his infirmities—which shows the verb is not sin in itself. The question is whether a man is displaying something he received or something he claims to have generated.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BOAST as to brag, to vaunt oneself, to speak with pride or exultation of one's own worth or possessions; and as a noun, a vaunting, or the cause of boasting.
webster_full: BOAST, v.i. — To brag, or vaunt one's self; to make an ostentatious display, in speech, of one's own worth, property, or actions.
BOAST, n. — Expression of ostentation, pride or vanity; a vaunting. Also, the cause of boasting; occasion of pride or laudable exultation.
scriptures: Thus saith the LORD, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches:
Where is boasting then? It is excluded. By what law? of works? Nay: but by the law of faith.
That, according as it is written, He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord.
But now ye rejoice in your boastings: all such rejoicing is evil.
corruption_summary: Boasting has been rehabilitated as personal branding—the curated highlight, the portfolio self, the humble-brag—so that the sustained public advertisement of one's own worth is now a job requirement rather than the thing Scripture says grace excludes.
corruption_paragraphs: The platform economy has made self-promotion a form of maintenance. A man is expected to publish his achievements continuously, and the one who does not is assumed to have none. The word boast survives only as a mild social offense—bragging too obviously—while the practice is universal and professionalized. Scripture attacks the root rather than the manners: boasting is excluded not because it is impolite but because grace has removed the grounds. A man who genuinely believes he contributed nothing to his own salvation has lost the raw material for the whole enterprise.

The subtler corruption is boasting laundered through gratitude. Blessed attached to a photograph of one's own success does the same work with better cover. Scripture's alternative is not silence about God's gifts but a redirected object: glory in the Lord, glory in the cross, glory even in infirmities, since those display strength that is plainly not one's own. James adds the timeline correction that no branding strategy accommodates: the man boasting about next year does not know whether he will be alive to see it.
roots_summary: Hebrew halal, to praise or make a show, from which comes hallelujah; Greek kauchaomai, to boast or glory—a verb that is holy or damning according to its object.
roots_lines: Hebrew halal (H1984) — to shine, praise, boast, make a show; the same root behind hallelujah, praise directed rightly (Ps 34:2; Prov 27:1; Jer 9:24).
Greek kauchaomai (G2744) — to boast, glory, exult; used both of forbidden self-glorying and of glorying in the Lord and in tribulations (Rom 5:3; 1 Cor 1:31; 2 Cor 12:9; Gal 6:14).
Greek kauchēma (G2745) — the ground or matter of boasting; what a man actually has to show (Rom 4:2; 1 Cor 9:15-16; Phil 2:16).
usage: Let him that glorieth glory in the Lord—the object is moved, not the verb removed.
Where is boasting then? It is excluded—justification by faith destroys the invoice.
James 4:16 answers the man who boasts about next year: it is not his to spend.

etymology: Latin obtinere: ob- (toward, against) + tenere (to hold)—to hold on to, to get possession of. The KJV uses it for what is received on promise and mercy far more than for what is seized by effort.
biblical_def: Obtain in the KJV covers getting, gaining, and coming into possession—but the striking pattern is what the objects are and how they arrive. Men obtain mercy, obtain promises, obtain salvation, obtain a good report, obtain an inheritance, obtain joy. Hebrews 11 lists it among the works of faith: Who through faith subdued kingdoms, wrought righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions (Heb 11:33)—obtaining stands in a series of active verbs, yet through faith governs the whole list. Paul is explicit that salvation is an appointment before it is an attainment: God hath not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation by our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Thess 5:9), and he endures everything that they may also obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory (2 Tim 2:10). Isaiah's ransomed come home and obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away (Isa 35:10)—joy obtained by ransom, not by pursuit. Scripture also knows the counterfeit: men who obtain the world and lose the soul, and Simon who thought the gift of God might be obtained with money. So the biblical logic is not passivity. Men run, strive, endure, and lay hold. But what they finally obtain was promised first, and the obtaining is faith taking hold of something already secured by Another.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines OBTAIN as to get, acquire, or procure—in a general sense, to gain possession of; noting the word implies desire and some effort, or the favor of another.
webster_full: OBTAIN, v.t. — To get; to gain; to procure; in a general sense, to gain possession of, either by effort or by request. Some things we obtain by labor; some by gift or favor.
OBTAIN, v.i. — To be received in customary use; to continue in use; to prevail; to be established. Also, to succeed; to prevail in a request.
scriptures: Who through faith subdued kingdoms, wrought righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions,
For God hath not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation by our Lord Jesus Christ,
Therefore I endure all things for the elect's sakes, that they may also obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory.
And the ransomed of the LORD shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads: they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away.
corruption_summary: Obtaining has been absorbed into the achievement stack—hustle on one side, manifestation on the other—both of which locate the power in the seeker, where Scripture locates it in the promise and the Promiser.
corruption_paragraphs: Two rival gospels of obtaining dominate the age and they are closer than they look. The grind school says a man obtains by output: enough hours, enough discipline, enough leverage. The manifestation school says he obtains by alignment: enough belief, enough visualization, enough energy sent out. Both agree that the operative power is inside the man, and both are refuted by the same sentence—God hath not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation by our Lord Jesus Christ. Appointment precedes obtaining.

The correction is not sloth. Hebrews 11 is a chapter of exertion, and Paul says he endures all things so that the elect may obtain. Scripture's men obtain by faith that works, not by faith instead of work. But when the object is mercy, promise, salvation or joy, the biblical grammar is consistently receptive: these are given, inherited, ransomed, appointed. A culture that only knows how to earn or to attract has no category for a gift that must simply be taken hold of.
roots_summary: Hebrew nasag, to reach or overtake; Greek epitynchanō, to hit the mark and so to obtain, and peripoiēsis, an obtaining or possession secured for one.
roots_lines: Hebrew nasag (H5381) — to reach, overtake, obtain; the ransomed obtain joy and gladness (Isa 35:10; 51:11; Gen 44:4).
Greek epitynchanō (G2013) — to hit upon, attain, obtain; used of Israel not obtaining what it sought (Rom 11:7; Heb 6:15; 11:33; Jas 4:2).
Greek peripoiēsis (G4047) — an acquiring or obtaining, hence a purchased possession; to obtain salvation in 1 Thess 5:9 (Eph 1:14; 2 Thess 2:14; 1 Pet 2:9).
usage: To obtain salvation by our Lord Jesus Christ—appointment first, obtaining second.
Hebrews 11:33 — they obtained promises, and the whole list runs on through faith.
The ransomed obtain joy: joy arriving by ransom, not by pursuit.

etymology: Old English hōre, from a Germanic root related to Latin carus, dear—one hired for love. The KJV uses the plain word and its family (whoredom, whoremonger, go a whoring) for both the sexual sin and the covenant sin it pictures.
biblical_def: The KJV uses whore in two joined registers, and refusing either one costs the reader the meaning of both. Literally, it names sexual sin sold or given outside covenant. The law forbids a father to make merchandise of his daughter: Do not prostitute thy daughter, to cause her to be a whore; lest the land fall to whoredom, and the land become full of wickedness (Lev 19:29)—a whole land corrupted by what begins in one household. Paul argues from union: Know ye not that your bodies are the members of Christ? shall I then take the members of Christ, and make them the members of an harlot? God forbid (1 Cor 6:15). Because the believer is joined to Christ, sexual sin is not a private appetite but a collision of unions. Figuratively—and this is the larger usage—the prophets call covenant unfaithfulness whoredom. Ezekiel's indictment of Jerusalem is a marriage betrayal: thou didst trust in thine own beauty, and playedst the harlot because of thy renown (Ezek 16:15). Hosea is commanded to live the picture. Revelation ends the theme with the great whore who sits on many waters (Rev 17:1), the counterfeit set against the Lamb's wife of Revelation 21. The Bible's sexual ethic and its doctrine of covenant are the same doctrine: God is a husband, idolatry is adultery, and the church is either a chaste bride or she is playing the harlot.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WHORE as a woman who practices unlawful commerce with men, especially for hire; and, in Scripture, a term for one who forsakes the true God for idols—idolatry being spiritual whoredom.
webster_full: WHORE, n. — A woman who practices unlawful commerce with men; a prostitute; a harlot. In Scripture, one who forsakes the true God and worships idols.
WHOREDOM, n. — Lewdness; fornication; the practice of unlawful commerce with the other sex. In Scripture, idolatry; the desertion of the worship of the true God for the worship of idols.
scriptures: Do not prostitute thy daughter, to cause her to be a whore; lest the land fall to whoredom, and the land become full of wickedness.
But thou didst trust in thine own beauty, and playedst the harlot because of thy renown, and pouredst out thy fornications on every one that passed by; his it was.
Know ye not that your bodies are the members of Christ? shall I then take the members of Christ, and make them the members of an harlot? God forbid.
And there came one of the seven angels which had the seven vials, and talked with me, saying unto me, Come hither; I will shew unto thee the judgment of the great whore that sitteth upon many waters:
corruption_summary: The word survives almost solely as an insult thrown at women, while the sin it names is treated as work or preference and the covenant sense has vanished—which is exactly backwards from Scripture, where the term is aimed hardest at God's own unfaithful people.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions run in opposite directions. The culture normalizes the trade—renaming it work, content, or empowerment—while keeping the word as a slur to fling at individual women. Scripture does neither. It refuses to soften what selling or spending the body outside covenant is, and it aims the accusation with startling frequency not at prostitutes but at the covenant people: Israel is the one who played the harlot. In the Gospels the actual prostitutes are told to go and sin no more and are received; the religious men who kept their reputations are the ones warned they will enter the kingdom last.

The second corruption is the loss of the figure. Once whoredom no longer names idolatry, the prophets become inexplicably harsh and the marriage imagery of Scripture becomes decorative. Keep it, and the logic snaps into place: God is a husband, His people are a bride, idolatry is infidelity, and Revelation's contrast between the great whore and the Lamb's wife is the last statement of a theme running from Sinai. A church that cannot say this word has no way to name what it is doing when it courts the world.
roots_summary: Hebrew zanah, to commit fornication and to go a whoring after idols; Greek pornē, a harlot, the root of pornography.
roots_lines: Hebrew zanah (H2181) — to commit fornication, play the harlot; used constantly of Israel going a whoring after other gods (Exod 34:15; Lev 19:29; Hos 1:2; Ezek 16:15).
Hebrew zenunim (H2183) — whoredoms, acts of infidelity, literal and spiritual (Gen 38:24; 2 Kgs 9:22; Hos 2:2).
Greek pornē (G4204) — a harlot; the root of porneia, fornication, and of the English pornography (Matt 21:31; 1 Cor 6:15-16; Rev 17:1).
usage: Make the members of Christ the members of an harlot? God forbid—union argues against the sin.
Ezekiel 16 aims the word at the covenant people, not at outsiders.
Revelation's great whore stands opposite the Lamb's wife: two brides, one ending.

etymology: Old French marchant, from Latin mercari, to trade, from merx, merchandise. The same root gives market, commerce, and mercy's false cousin mercenary—the trader is one who deals for gain.
biblical_def: Scripture treats trade as lawful and the trader as accountable. The virtuous woman is commended in commercial terms: She is like the merchants' ships; she bringeth her food from afar, and she makes fine linen and sells it (Prov 31:14, 24). Solomon trades, Tyre grows rich by trade, and nothing in the law forbids buying and selling. What the law forbids is the dishonest weight, the shifted landmark, and the sabbath turned into a market day. The prophets indict Tyre not for merchandising but for the pride and violence that came with it, and Revelation's merchants weep over Babylon because their market is gone, having trafficked at the last in the souls of men (Rev 18:11). Christ uses the merchant twice, in both directions. Positively, the kingdom itself is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls: who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it (Matt 13:45-46)—a shrewd trader who liquidates the entire portfolio for one asset, which is commended as wisdom rather than folly. Negatively, He clears the temple: make not my Father's house an house of merchandise (John 2:16). The line is drawn not between commerce and holiness but between the market's proper field and the one place where it may not set up its tables.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MERCHANT as one who traffics or carries on trade with foreign countries, or who buys and sells goods as a business—a trafficker, a trader.
webster_full: MERCHANT, n. — A man who traffics or carries on trade with foreign countries, or who exports and imports goods and sells them by wholesale.
MERCHANDISE, n. — The objects of commerce; wares, goods, commodities; whatever is usually bought or sold in trade. Make not my Father's house an house of merchandise (John 2:16).
scriptures: She is like the merchants' ships; she bringeth her food from afar.
Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls:
And said unto them that sold doves, Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise.
And the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her; for no man buyeth their merchandise any more:
corruption_summary: The market has stopped being a field and become a total environment—worship, friendship, attention, identity and the body all priced—so that the temple-clearing has no boundary left to defend and even ministry is measured as merchandise.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture's problem is never commerce as such; it is commerce with no perimeter. Christ did not condemn the sellers for selling but for where they had set up. The modern condition is that there is no where left: attention is sold, friendship is monetized, the body is content, and churches are evaluated by metrics indistinguishable from a retailer's. Revelation's list of Babylon's cargo ends with slaves, and souls of men, which is the terminal form of a market that recognizes no boundary—persons themselves become inventory.

The mirror-image corruption inside the church is a spirituality that despises trade altogether, treating profit as inherently dirty and the businessman as a second-class disciple. Proverbs 31 refutes it: the woman most praised in the wisdom literature runs ships, buys fields, and sells linen. And Christ's own picture of the kingdom is a merchant doing the shrewdest trade of his life. The call is not to leave the market but to keep it out of the sanctuary and to trade with honest weights.
roots_summary: Hebrew sachar, to travel about for trade, hence merchant; Greek emporos, a traveling trader—the root of emporium.
roots_lines: Hebrew sachar (H5503) — to go about, trade, traffic; the participle is the common word for merchant (Gen 23:16; Prov 31:14; Ezek 27:12-36).
Hebrew kena‘ani (H3669) — Canaanite, and by extension trafficker or merchant, since Canaan was the trading nation (Prov 31:24; Hos 12:7; Zech 14:21).
Greek emporos (G1713) — one on a journey for trade, a merchant; used of the pearl merchant and of Babylon's traders (Matt 13:45; Rev 18:3, 11, 15).
usage: The kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man—shrewd trading commended, not condemned.
Make not my Father's house an house of merchandise—the market has a field, and a fence.
Proverbs 31 praises a woman who runs ships and sells linen; trade is not the sin.

etymology: Latin instruere: in- (in, upon) + struere (to build, pile up)—to build into. The same root gives structure. To instruct is to build something into a man, not merely to inform him.
biblical_def: To instruct is to build teaching into a person with authority and for a purpose. Proverbs opens by naming instruction as the point of the whole book—to know wisdom and instruction, to receive the instruction of wisdom—and it assumes a household: a father instructing a son who is expected to obey rather than evaluate. The wise man's mark is that he takes it: Hear counsel, and receive instruction, that thou mayest be wise in thy latter end (Prov 19:20). The whole of Scripture is given for it: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness (2 Tim 3:16)—four uses, of which three correct and only one merely teaches. Paul also names instruction's counterfeit, the man who is instructed out of the law and confident he is a guide to the blind while dishonoring God by breaking it (Rom 2:18-23). Instruction received without obedience produces a worse man, not a better one. Elsewhere instruct carries the sense of equipping or ordering, and the Psalms use it of God Himself: I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go. The consistent picture is vertical—God to man, father to son, elder to younger—and always aimed at conduct rather than at information.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines INSTRUCT as to teach; to inform the mind; to educate; to direct or furnish with orders; and to build up, from the Latin sense of building into.
webster_full: INSTRUCT, v.t. — To teach; to inform the mind; to educate; to impart knowledge to one who was destitute of it. Instruct him in the way he should go.
INSTRUCT, v.t. — To direct; to enjoin; to furnish with orders, as an agent or a jury. Also, to model; to form; to prepare.
scriptures: Hear counsel, and receive instruction, that thou mayest be wise in thy latter end.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
And knowest his will, and approvest the things that are more excellent, being instructed out of the law;
corruption_summary: Instruction has been recast as an insult to autonomy—being told what to do treated as disrespect—so that a culture full of information has almost no one willing to be built into by anybody.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning instinct is that no one may instruct anyone. Teaching is acceptable if offered as one perspective among many; correction is an imposition; and the phrase don't tell me what to do functions as a moral position rather than an adolescent complaint. Proverbs has a word for the man who will not be instructed, and the word is not independent. Folly in Proverbs is not stupidity but unteachability—the refusal to receive from someone with standing to give it.

The opposite error is real and worth naming: instruction that is only content delivery. A culture drowning in explanation, courses and commentary can be endlessly informed and never instructed, because instruction in the biblical sense is built into conduct and verified there. Paul's warning in Romans 2 is exactly this—a man thoroughly instructed out of the law, confident as a guide to others, dishonoring God by his own life. Information received without obedience does not leave a man neutral. It leaves him worse.
roots_summary: Hebrew musar, instruction that includes correction, and yarah, to point or teach, the root of torah; Greek paideia, the training of a child.
roots_lines: Hebrew musar (H4148) — instruction, discipline, chastening; Proverbs' key word, in which teaching and correction are one thing (Prov 1:2, 7; 19:20; Job 36:10).
Hebrew yarah (H3384) — to throw, point, direct, teach; the root behind torah, instruction (Exod 24:12; Ps 32:8; Isa 2:3).
Greek paideia (G3809) — the whole training and education of a child, including correction; instruction in righteousness (Eph 6:4; 2 Tim 3:16; Heb 12:5-11).
usage: Hear counsel, and receive instruction—the wise man is the one who takes it.
2 Timothy 3:16 gives four uses of Scripture; three of them correct.
Romans 2:18 — instructed out of the law and dishonoring God by breaking it.

etymology: Old English gerecenian, to recount or arrange in order. The KJV uses it as an accounting word—to count, compute, impute—rendering Greek logizomai, a term drawn straight from the ledger.
biblical_def: Reckon is a bookkeeping word, and Paul builds the doctrine of justification on it. Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness (Rom 4:3)—the same verb Paul repeats eleven times in that chapter, arguing that righteousness was entered into Abraham's account rather than earned by his work. From that ledger comes the command of Romans 6:11: Likewise reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord. This is not visualization or positive thinking. Reckoning is counting as true what God has already declared true; a man does not make himself dead to sin by reckoning, he does the arithmetic God has already done. Paul reckons about suffering the same way: I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us (Rom 8:18)—an explicit weighing of two quantities, one visible and one promised. And the verb falls on Christ Himself: he was reckoned among the transgressors (Luke 22:37), the great exchange stated in ledger terms—our account charged to Him, His righteousness credited to us. The whole gospel can be told in this one verb.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines RECKON as to count; to number; to compute; to esteem or account; and to charge to account—the language of a settled reckoning.
webster_full: RECKON, v.t. — To count; to number; to enumerate; to compute; that is, to tell the particulars of a sum.
RECKON, v.t. — To esteem; to account; to repute; to charge to account. He was reckoned among the transgressors (Luke 22:37). Hence, to reckon with, to settle accounts.
scriptures: For what saith the scripture? Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness.
Likewise reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord.
For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.
For I say unto you, that this that is written must yet be accomplished in me, And he was reckoned among the transgressors: for the things concerning me have an end.
corruption_summary: Reckon has decayed into a shrug—a regional filler meaning I suppose—which strips the accounting force out of the verb Paul uses to state justification, mortification, and the great exchange.
corruption_paragraphs: In current English I reckon signals a mild guess. In Paul it signals a ledger entry that is either accurate or fraudulent. When Romans 6:11 is read with the modern sense, the command sounds like an invitation to think positively about one's spiritual condition—which is why so many believers try to feel dead to sin and conclude they have failed. With the accounting sense restored the command is far more solid and far less exhausting: God has recorded the believer as dead to sin and alive to God in Christ; reckoning is agreeing with the entry and living off the balance.

The second corruption is the therapeutic near-miss that borrows the mechanism and removes the Accountant. Speaking things into existence, declaring one's identity, affirming a truth until it becomes true—these locate the creative power in the speaker. Biblical reckoning is strictly derivative. It counts as true only what God has already declared, which is why it can bear weight in a hospital room where affirmation collapses.
roots_summary: Hebrew chashab, to reckon, impute, or account; Greek logizomai, to count or credit—a commercial term Paul makes the vehicle of justification.
roots_lines: Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to reckon, account, impute; he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness (Gen 15:6; Ps 32:2).
Greek logizomai (G3049) — to count, compute, credit to an account; eleven times in Romans 4, and again in Rom 6:11 and 8:18 (2 Cor 5:19; Gal 3:6; Jas 2:23).
Greek ellogeo (G1677) — to charge to one's account; Paul's word to Philemon, put that on mine account (Rom 5:13; Phm 1:18).
usage: Reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin—agreeing with God's entry, not manufacturing a feeling.
Romans 4 uses the ledger verb eleven times: righteousness credited, not earned.
He was reckoned among the transgressors—the exchange stated in accounting terms.

etymology: Latin creare, to bring forth, produce, beget. In the KJV it renders Hebrew bara, a verb whose subject in the Old Testament is never anyone but God—a grammatical fact that carries a doctrine.
biblical_def: In Scripture, to create is what God does and what no creature does. The Hebrew bara is used some fifty times, and in every one God is the subject; men build, form, make, fashion and beget, but they do not create. The Bible opens with it: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth (Gen 1:1)—no pre-existing material named, no assistant credited. It is used again at the summit of the sixth day, three times in one verse for emphasis: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them (Gen 1:27). Man's nature, his image-bearing, and his being made male and female are all inside the creating act, which is why they are not his to renegotiate. Isaiah presses the point against every rival: I have made the earth, and created man upon it: I, even my hands, have stretched out the heavens (Isa 45:12), in a passage that mocks the clay for arguing with the potter. The New Testament assigns the work to Christ: by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth... all things were created by him, and for him (Col 1:16). And the verb reappears in salvation, which Scripture treats as a second creation of the same order: we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works (Eph 2:10). A man cannot create himself the first time or the second.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CREATE as to produce; to bring into being from nothing; to cause to exist—and secondarily to make or form by investing with a new character, as to create a peer.
webster_full: CREATE, v.t. — To produce; to bring into being from nothing; to cause to exist. In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth (Gen 1:1).
CREATE, v.t. — To make or form, by investing with a new character; as, to create a peer. Also, to produce; to cause; to be the occasion of; as, to create confidence.
scriptures: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.

For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him:
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.
corruption_summary: The verb has been handed to the creature: men now speak of creating themselves, their truth, their gender and their reality—taking the one word Scripture reserves for God alone and making it the banner of self-definition.
corruption_paragraphs: Ordinary usage has diluted create until it means little more than make—creating a document, a playlist, content. That drift is harmless enough. The serious corruption is ontological: the claim that a person creates himself. Create your own truth, create your identity, create the life you want. Scripture's grammar forecloses it before the argument starts, because bara never takes a human subject. Men are creatures the whole way down. What God made in the creating act—image-bearing, and male and female—is given, and the clay does not get a vote on the potter's work.

The distinction to keep is the one the older language kept: God creates, man makes. Human making is real, dignified, and commanded—cultivate the garden, build the ark, weave the curtains, write the psalm. It is the image-bearer doing in miniature what his Maker does infinitely, but always with material already given. When a culture forgets that difference it does not become more creative; it becomes unable to receive anything, since everything must now be self-authored. And it has no answer for Ephesians 2:10, where even the new self is created in Christ Jesus by someone else's hand.
roots_summary: Hebrew bara, to create, whose subject is always God; Greek ktizō, to create or found—the verb of Colossians 1:16 and Ephesians 2:10.
roots_lines: Hebrew bara (H1254) — to create, shape, bring into being; used with God as subject only, never of human making (Gen 1:1, 21, 27; Isa 43:1; 45:12).
Hebrew asah (H6213) — to make, do, fashion from existing material; the verb men share with God (Gen 1:7; Exod 25:8).
Greek ktizō (G2936) — to create, found, bring into existence; used of the first creation and of the new man in Christ (Mark 13:19; Eph 2:10; Col 1:16; Rev 4:11).
usage: In the beginning God created—no material named, no assistant credited.
Genesis 1:27 puts the image and male-and-female inside the creating act.
God creates; man makes. The clay does not vote on the potter's work.

etymology: Latin nobilis, well-known, high-born, from noscere, to know—originally the family everyone knows. The KJV keeps both the birth sense and the character sense, and Acts 17 quietly transfers the honor from the first to the second.
biblical_def: Noble in the KJV first means high-born or high-ranked, and Scripture is candid that such men are rarely the ones God calls: ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called (1 Cor 1:26). The kingdom does not recruit from the top of the social register. But the word's most important use redefines nobility outright. Luke says of the Jews at Berea, These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so (Acts 17:11). Their nobility had nothing to do with birth, wealth or rank. It consisted of two things: an open readiness to hear, and a daily labor of checking what they heard against Scripture—even when the preacher was the apostle Paul. Teachability and verification, together, are what Scripture calls noble. Isaiah supplies the Old Testament parallel in a verse about generosity of soul: the liberal deviseth liberal things; and by liberal things shall he stand (Isa 32:8), where the noble man is marked by what he plans for others. Nehemiah records the counterexample—nobles who would not put their necks to the work of the Lord while everyone else built the wall. Rank without labor is not nobility in Scripture; it is an indictment.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines NOBLE as great, elevated, dignified; illustrious; exalted in rank or excellence of character; magnanimous; and as a noun, a person of rank above a commoner.
webster_full: NOBLE, a. — Great; elevated; dignified; being above every thing that can dishonor reputation; as a noble mind; a noble courage.
NOBLE, a. — Of an ancient and splendid family; of high rank in society. Also, magnanimous; generous; liberal; as a noble heart.
NOBLE, n. — A person of rank above a commoner; a nobleman.
scriptures: These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called:
But the liberal deviseth liberal things; and by liberal things shall he stand.
corruption_summary: Nobility now attaches to visibility—celebrity, platform, or the right public opinions—while Acts 17 assigns it to two unglamorous habits: a mind ready to receive, and daily verification of what it is told against Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern aristocracy is one of attention. Fame confers moral standing; a large audience is treated as evidence of worth, and public alignment with the correct position substitutes for character. Scripture's test is stubbornly private and repetitive. The Bereans were called noble for reading, daily, with an open mind and a checking pen, and no one would have known they were doing it. There is no way to perform Berean nobility for an audience, which is exactly why it is worth something.

The second corruption runs inside the church: nobility of soul confused with agreeableness. Being more noble in Acts 17 involved verifying an apostle's preaching against the text—an act that looks, from the platform, like insufficient trust. Luke commends it without qualification. And Nehemiah's nobles are a permanent warning in the other direction: men of rank who would not put their necks to the work while the goldsmiths and merchants built. Rank that will not labor is not nobility but its counterfeit.
roots_summary: Hebrew nadib, willing, generous, noble—a word about a liberal spirit before it is about rank; Greek eugenēs, well-born, used comparatively of the Bereans.
roots_lines: Hebrew nadib (H5081) — noble, willing, generous; rooted in a verb meaning to volunteer, so nobility is first a freely offered spirit (Exod 35:5; 1 Sam 2:8; Isa 32:8).
Hebrew chor (H2715) — a noble, one free-born; Nehemiah's nobles who would not work (Neh 3:5; 6:17; Jer 27:20).
Greek eugenēs (G2104) — well-born, high in rank, and by extension noble-minded; more noble than those in Thessalonica (Luke 19:12; Acts 17:11; 1 Cor 1:26).
usage: More noble... in that they received the word... and searched the scriptures daily—the biblical test.
Not many noble are called—the kingdom does not recruit from the top of the register.
Nehemiah's nobles would not put their necks to the work; rank that will not labor is a counterfeit.

etymology: Old English thorn, a spine or prickle, from a common Germanic root. In Scripture the thorn is a curse-marker: it appears the moment the ground is cursed, and it is still on the King's head at the crucifixion.
biblical_def: The thorn enters Scripture as a token of the curse. God tells Adam the ground will resist him: Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee (Gen 3:18). From that point thorns mark cursed and unfruitful ground throughout the prophets, choke the seed in the parable of the sower, and stand for the neighbors Israel failed to drive out: those which ye let remain of them shall be pricks in your eyes, and thorns in your sides (Num 33:55)—the compromise you tolerate becomes the thorn you carry. Then the picture turns twice. First in Paul, where a thorn becomes an instrument of grace rather than only of curse: there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted above measure (2 Cor 12:7). He asks three times for its removal and is refused, with the answer that has held up ten thousand sickbeds since: My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor 12:9). The thorn stays; the grace is given for it. Second, and decisively, at the cross: when they had platted a crown of thorns, they put it upon his head (Matt 27:29). The soldiers meant it as mockery. Scripture lets the symbol speak—the curse of Eden pressed onto the brow of the Second Adam, worn by the only man who never earned it.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines THORN as a tree or shrub armed with spines; the spine or sharp process itself; and figuratively, anything troublesome—a cumbrous care, a grievance, whatever pricks or annoys.
webster_full: THORN, n. — A tree or shrub armed with spines or sharp shoots; also, the sharp process itself from the woody part of a plant.
THORN, n. — Anything troublesome; in Scripture, great difficulties, embarrassments, or afflictions. A thorn in the flesh (2 Cor 12:7). Also, cares of this world, which choke the word.
scriptures: Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field;

And lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted above measure.

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
And when they had platted a crown of thorns, they put it upon his head, and a reed in his right hand: and they bowed the knee before him, and mocked him, saying, Hail, King of the Jews!
corruption_summary: The age holds that every thorn must come out—pain treated as a malfunction to be optimized away—leaving no framework for the thorn God gives, refuses to remove, and supplies grace to carry.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern assumptions run in a straight line: discomfort signals something wrong, something wrong can be fixed, and unfixed suffering means someone failed. Applied to faith it produces the teaching that any remaining thorn is evidence of insufficient belief. Paul's account destroys it. He knows the thorn's origin (a messenger of Satan), its divine purpose (lest he be exalted above measure), and the answer to his three requests, which was no. The thorn was given, and the grace was given with it. Some thorns stay until glory, and the man carrying one is not thereby a second-class Christian.

The opposite corruption is a piety that romanticizes affliction and refuses ordinary help—declining the physician, the counselor or the medication as though the thorn were holy in itself. Paul prayed three times for removal, which is neither stoicism nor resignation. He asked, and kept asking, until God answered. Scripture also keeps the third sense in view: Numbers 33 warns that a tolerated compromise becomes a thorn in the side, which means not every thorn is sent—some are simply the harvest of what was not driven out.
roots_summary: Hebrew qots, thorn or brier, the curse-word of Genesis 3; Greek skolops, a stake or splinter—Paul's thorn—and akantha, the thorn of the crown.
roots_lines: Hebrew qots (H6975) — thorns, briers; first named in the curse on the ground (Gen 3:18; Jer 4:3; Ezek 28:24).
Greek skolops (G4647) — a pointed stake or splinter; Paul's thorn in the flesh, a word suggesting something driven in rather than a surface prick (2 Cor 12:7).
Greek akantha (G173) — a thorn or bramble; the thorns that choke the seed and the crown platted for Christ (Matt 13:7, 22; 27:29; Heb 6:8).
usage: Thorns also and thistles—the thorn enters with the curse on the ground.
My grace is sufficient for thee—the answer given when the thorn is not removed.
Numbers 33:55 — the compromise you leave standing becomes the thorn in your side.

etymology: Old French bribe, a piece of bread given to a beggar; the sense slid from alms to extortion to the corrupt gift. The KJV usually calls it simply a gift—which is precisely how a bribe presents itself.
biblical_def: A bribe in Scripture is a gift that bends judgment, and the law's language is deliberately unglamorous: it is almost always called a gift, because that is what it looks like from the inside. The prohibition is absolute and comes with an explanation of the mechanism: thou shalt take no gift: for the gift blindeth the wise, and perverteth the words of the righteous (Exod 23:8). Note what it does not say. It does not say the gift blinds fools or corrupts the already-wicked; it says it blinds the wise and perverts the righteous. No one is constitutionally immune. Deuteronomy repeats it in the charge to judges, alongside the ban on wresting judgment and respecting persons (Deut 16:19). Proverbs describes the transaction's discretion: A wicked man taketh a gift out of the bosom to pervert the ways of judgment (Prov 17:23)—out of the bosom, from inside the robe, unseen. Isaiah indicts a whole ruling class in one line: Thy princes are rebellious, and companions of thieves: every one loveth gifts, and followeth after rewards: they judge not the fatherless, neither doth the cause of the widow come unto them (Isa 1:23). The tell is always the same and it is never the rhetoric: watch who stops getting justice. When the fatherless and the widow can no longer get a hearing, the gifts have already done their work.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BRIBE as a price, reward, gift or favor bestowed or promised to pervert the judgment or corrupt the conduct of a judge, witness, or other person—and notes that a bribe may be anything that gains an improper influence.
webster_full: BRIBE, n. — A price, reward, gift or favor bestowed or promised with a view to pervert the judgment, or corrupt the conduct of a judge, witness or other person. A gift blindeth the eyes of the wise (Deut 16:19).
BRIBE, v.t. — To give or promise a reward or consideration, with a view to pervert the judgment or corrupt the conduct. Also, that which seduces; whatever gains an improper influence over the mind.
scriptures: And thou shalt take no gift: for the gift blindeth the wise, and perverteth the words of the righteous.
Thou shalt not wrest judgment; thou shalt not respect persons, neither take a gift: for a gift doth blind the eyes of the wise, and pervert the words of the righteous.
A wicked man taketh a gift out of the bosom to pervert the ways of judgment.
Thy princes are rebellious, and companions of thieves: every one loveth gifts, and followeth after rewards: they judge not the fatherless, neither doth the cause of the widow come unto them.
corruption_summary: Bribery has been rebranded rather than abolished—access, consulting fees, speaking honoraria, gifted product, platform deals—and because no envelope changes hands, men who would never take a bribe take one weekly and never suspect it.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instruments are cleaner than cash and work the same way: the sponsorship that makes a criticism awkward, the free trip that buys a favorable review, the retainer that arrives before the vote, the platform access that would evaporate if the wrong thing were said. Exodus 23:8 is not a rule about envelopes; it is a claim about human wiring. The gift blinds the wise. A man who believes himself incorruptible has simply lost the ability to notice the moment his judgment moved, which is what the verse says will happen.

The two most useful biblical tests both survive translation. The first is Proverbs' phrase—out of the bosom. If a transaction must be kept out of sight to keep working, it is already the thing. The second is Isaiah's: bribery is measured by who stops getting justice. When the fatherless and the widow can no longer get a hearing, no one has to prove the gifts changed hands; the docket has already testified. A church, a court, or a household can be audited by that same test.
roots_summary: Hebrew shochad, a gift given to secure a verdict; Greek dōron, a gift, and the verb-family behind Felix's hope of money from Paul.
roots_lines: Hebrew shochad (H7810) — a present, especially one given to pervert judgment; the standard word rendered gift in the bribery statutes (Exod 23:8; Deut 16:19; 1 Sam 8:3; Ps 26:10).
Hebrew betsa (H1215) — unjust gain, covetous profit; what the bribe-taking judge is after (Exod 18:21; Prov 1:19; Isa 33:15).
Greek dōron (G1435) — a gift or present; the neutral word whose corrupt use Scripture exposes, as when Felix hoped money would be given him by Paul (Acts 24:26).
usage: The gift blindeth the wise—the warning is aimed at the wise, not the corrupt.
Out of the bosom—if it must stay unseen to work, it is already a bribe.
Isaiah's test: watch who stops getting a hearing. The docket testifies.

etymology: Latin adornare: ad- (to) + ornare (to furnish, decorate)—the root of ornament and, further back, of order. To adorn is to set in order so as to make beautiful, not merely to cover.
biblical_def: To adorn is to make beautiful by ordering, and Scripture is neither embarrassed by beauty nor neutral about what is being displayed. Isaiah uses it of salvation itself in unashamedly festive terms: he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation... as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels (Isa 61:10). Beauty is not the problem. The apostolic instruction concerns proportion and direction. Paul writes that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array (1 Tim 2:9), and the following verse supplies the substitute—good works, which is what he actually wants them adorned with. Peter says the same with a jeweler's phrase: the true ornament is the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price (1 Pet 3:4). He does not say the visible is worthless; he says the imperishable is the valuable one. And Titus extends adorning past clothing altogether: bondservants, by honesty and fidelity in ordinary work, adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things (Titus 2:10). That is the widest use—a life can be the ornament that makes a doctrine look like what it is. The question Scripture asks of any adorning is simply what it is advertising.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ADORN as to deck or decorate; to make beautiful; to add to beauty by dress or ornaments; and to display the beauty or excellence of a thing.
webster_full: ADORN, v.t. — To deck or decorate; to make beautiful; to add to beauty by dress; to deck with external ornaments.

ADORN, v.t. — To set off to advantage; to add ornaments to; to embellish by any thing external or adventitious; to display the beauty or excellence of. That they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour (Titus 2:10).
scriptures: In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;
Not purloining, but shewing all good fidelity; that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things.
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.

I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels.
corruption_summary: Adorning has become total self-presentation—the body as the entire message, curated and published continuously—while Scripture asks what the ornament is advertising and answers with good works, a quiet spirit, and a doctrine made visible.
corruption_paragraphs: The platform age turned adorning into a full-time occupation with an audience attached. Appearance is no longer preparation for a life; it is the product. The apostolic correction is not a dress code but a redirection: Paul's not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls is followed immediately by what he does want on display—good works. Peter names the imperishable ornament, the meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price—a valuation deliberately stated in jeweler's terms against a market that prices the other thing.

The opposite corruption is a sourness that treats beauty as suspect and drabness as holiness. Isaiah blows that away: salvation itself is described as a bridegroom decking himself and a bride putting on her jewels, and the tabernacle was made for glory and for beauty. Scripture's issue is never that a woman is lovely or a room is beautiful; it is proportion and direction. Titus supplies the widest and most searching form—an honest worker who does not pilfer adorns the doctrine, which means a life can make the gospel look like what it actually is, or like something else.
roots_summary: Greek kosmeō, to arrange, order, adorn—the root of cosmos and cosmetic; Hebrew adah, to deck oneself with ornaments.
roots_lines: Greek kosmeō (G2885) — to put in order, arrange, adorn; the same root as kosmos, the ordered world, so adorning is ordering into beauty (Matt 12:44; 1 Tim 2:9; Titus 2:10; Rev 21:2).
Greek kosmos (G2889) — order, ornament, and hence the world; used for adorning in 1 Pet 3:3, where the outward adorning is contrasted with the hidden man of the heart.
Hebrew adah (H5710) — to ornament, deck oneself; used of the bride adorning herself with jewels (Isa 61:10; Jer 4:30; Ezek 16:11).
usage: Adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour—an honest worker's life as the ornament.
The ornament of a meek and quiet spirit—priced by God, in jeweler's language.
Isaiah 61:10 — salvation described as a bride putting on her jewels. Beauty is not the problem.

etymology: Latin seducere: se- (aside, apart) + ducere (to lead)—to lead aside. The KJV keeps the leading-away sense, and applies it to doctrine at least as often as to chastity.
biblical_def: To seduce is to lead someone aside from the path, and in the KJV the path is usually doctrinal before it is sexual. Christ warns that false Christs and false prophets shall rise, and shall shew signs and wonders, to seduce, if it were possible, even the elect (Mark 13:22)—seduction here comes with credentials and miracles, not with an obvious lie. John writes to a church under pressure: These things have I written unto you concerning them that seduce you (1 John 2:26), and his antidote is the anointing that teaches, not merely stronger willpower. Paul describes the trajectory: evil men and seducers shall wax worse and worse, deceiving, and being deceived (2 Tim 3:13)—a line that names the seducer's own fate. He is not standing outside the deception operating it; he is inside it, going down with the thing he sells. The Old Testament uses the word of leading Israel astray into idolatry, and Proverbs 7 gives the sexual form at full length—the young man led along with smooth speech until he goes as an ox goeth to the slaughter, a passage careful to show that the seduction was verbal and gradual long before it was physical. That is the biblical anatomy: seduction is not force, it is guidance. Someone is being walked, agreeably, one step at a time, off the road.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SEDUCE as to draw aside or entice from the path of rectitude and duty; to lead astray; to corrupt; to entice to a surrender of chastity.
webster_full: SEDUCE, v.t. — To draw aside or entice from the path of rectitude and duty in any manner, by flattery, promises, bribes or otherwise; to tempt and lead to iniquity; to corrupt; to deprave.
SEDUCE, v.t. — To entice to a surrender of chastity. Hence SEDUCER, one who leads astray; one who entices from virtue or duty.
scriptures: For false Christs and false prophets shall rise, and shall shew signs and wonders, to seduce, if it were possible, even the elect.
But evil men and seducers shall wax worse and worse, deceiving, and being deceived.
These things have I written unto you concerning them that seduce you.
corruption_summary: Seduction has been narrowed to a romantic genre and even flattered as skill, while its doctrinal sense—being led aside from truth by teachers with signs and credentials—has dropped out of ordinary speech entirely.
corruption_paragraphs: In current usage seduction is either an erotic category or a compliment about persuasive charm. Scripture's primary use is neither. The seducers of Mark 13 and 1 John are teachers, and they arrive with wonders, plausibility and warmth—which is what makes the warning necessary. If false teaching announced itself, no one would need to be warned. The loss of the doctrinal sense leaves a church that can recognize a scandal but not a drift, and drift is what the word actually names.

Two features of the biblical account are worth keeping. First, seduction operates by leading rather than seizing, so consent at every step is the method, not a defense. Proverbs 7 lingers on the smooth speech precisely because nothing was forced. Second, Paul's line runs both directions: seducers deceiving, and being deceived. The man doing the leading is not a cynic in control of the scheme; he is further down the same road, which is why exposure so rarely produces repentance and why the only real protection is not cleverness but the truth already taught.
roots_summary: Greek planaō, to lead astray or cause to wander—the root of planet, a wandering star; Hebrew ta‘ah, to err or stray.
roots_lines: Greek planaō (G4105) — to lead astray, cause to wander, deceive; the root behind planet, the wandering star (Matt 24:4-5; Mark 13:22; 1 John 2:26; Rev 12:9).
Greek planē (G4106) — the wandering itself, error, delusion; the state a seducer produces (Eph 4:14; 2 Thess 2:11; 2 Pet 3:17).
Hebrew ta‘ah (H8582) — to err, wander, stray; used of prophets who cause the people to err (Isa 53:6; Jer 23:13, 32).
usage: False Christs... shall shew signs and wonders, to seduce—seduction arrives with credentials.
Deceiving, and being deceived—the seducer is inside the deception, not above it.
Seduction leads; it does not seize. Consent at every step is the method, not the defense.

etymology: Latin adulter, one who corrupts another's marriage, from ad- (to) + alter (other)—to turn toward another. This entry treats the person; the act has its own page.
biblical_def: An adulterer is the man—and the adulteress the woman—who breaks the marriage covenant sexually. This page treats the person; for the act and its ethic see Adultery. The seventh commandment is four words in English: Thou shalt not commit adultery (Exod 20:14). The Mosaic penalty names both parties without distinction of sex, which was itself remarkable in the ancient world: the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death (Lev 20:10). Christ then extends the category inward without softening it: whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart (Matt 5:28)—which makes the label reach a great many respectable men who have never touched anyone. Paul lists adulterers among those who shall not inherit the kingdom of God (1 Cor 6:9), and then, four verses later, says of that whole catalogue, and such were some of you: but ye are washed—the single most important sentence for anyone reading this page about himself. The word is a description of what a man has done, not a permanent species he belongs to. Hebrews states the standing judgment plainly: Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge (Heb 13:4). Two things are said in one breath—the marriage bed is honorable and clean, and God Himself is the judge of those who defile it. No human tribunal is named, which means the sin is never actually unwitnessed.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ADULTERER as a man guilty of adultery—one who has criminal intercourse with a married woman not his wife; and in Scripture, an idolater, or an apostate from the true faith.
webster_full: ADULTERER, n. — A man guilty of adultery; a man who has sexual commerce with any married woman, except his wife.

ADULTERER, n. — In Scripture, an idolater; also, an apostate from the true faith, or one who violates his covenant engagements; a very wicked person. Ye adulterers and adulteresses, know ye not that the friendship of the world is enmity with God (Jas 4:4).
scriptures: And the man that committeth adultery with another man's wife, even he that committeth adultery with his neighbour's wife, the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death.
But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.
Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.
corruption_summary: The category has been dissolved by consent—arrangements, openness, and the claim that pornography involves no one—while Christ's ruling makes the label reach the private man who has broken no vow visibly and broken it thoroughly in the heart.
corruption_paragraphs: The dissolving move is procedural: if all parties agree, no one has been wronged, and the word becomes an anachronism describing a bookkeeping error in an outdated contract. Scripture's marriage is not a contract between two adults but a covenant witnessed by God, which is why Hebrews 13:4 names God as the judge rather than a court or a spouse. Consent cannot license what was never the parties' to trade. The second dissolving move is technological—pornography treated as private and victimless—and Matthew 5:28 answers it directly and uncomfortably: the adultery is already accomplished in the heart, with a real person on the other side of the screen.

The church's own corruption runs the other way, and this page must say so plainly. Adulterer gets used as a permanent caste marker, a label pinned to a man for life. Paul's list in 1 Corinthians 6 includes adulterers among those who will not inherit the kingdom—and then says such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified. Past tense. The gospel does not soften what adultery is; it moves men out of the category. A church that keeps the label after God has removed it is preaching a different message than the one Paul preached to men who had done exactly this.
roots_summary: Hebrew na'aph, to commit adultery, used of marital and covenant infidelity; Greek moichos, an adulterer, and moicheuō, the verb of the seventh commandment.
roots_lines: Hebrew na'aph (H5003) — to commit adultery; used both of the marital sin and of Israel's idolatry (Exod 20:14; Jer 3:8-9; Hos 4:13).
Greek moichos (G3432) — an adulterer; the noun in Paul's and the writer to the Hebrews' warnings (Luke 18:11; 1 Cor 6:9; Heb 13:4).
Greek moicheuō (G3431) — to commit adultery; the verb of the seventh commandment and of Christ's extension of it to the look (Matt 5:27-28; Rom 2:22; Jas 2:11).
usage: Person, not act — the ethic lives on the Adultery page; this is the man who does it.
Leviticus 20:10 names both parties: adulterer and adulteress alike.
Such were some of you: but ye are washed—the label is what a man did, not what he must remain.

etymology: Latin distribuere: dis- (apart) + tribuere (to allot, assign, pay)—originally to divide among the tribes. To distribute is to divide a thing out to those it is assigned to.
biblical_def: To distribute is to divide out what one holds so that others receive. Christ's word to the rich young ruler is the sharpest form: sell all that thou hast, and distribute unto the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven (Luke 18:22)—a command aimed at one man's specific idol, and a test he failed. In the early church distribution becomes a structure rather than an impulse: believers laid the proceeds of sold property at the apostles' feet, and distribution was made unto every man according as he had need (Acts 4:35). Two things about that passage resist modern misuse in both directions. The giving was voluntary—Peter tells Ananias the land was his own and the money was in his own power—and the distributing was accountable, done by named men before the whole church, by need rather than by equal shares. Paul makes it ordinary Christian practice, not an emergency measure: Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality (Rom 12:13), and he charges the rich that they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate (1 Tim 6:18). Note that Paul does not tell the rich to stop being rich; he tells them to become ready to distribute, which is a disposition of the hand rather than a one-time transaction. The same verb governs the Spirit's gifts, dividing to every man severally as he will (1 Cor 12:11)—distribution as God's own habit, and never equal shares.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DISTRIBUTE as to divide among two or more; to deal out; to apportion, as in dividing a thing into parts and assigning each part to the proper person.
webster_full: DISTRIBUTE, v.t. — To divide among two or more; to deal out; to apportion to individuals; as, to distribute the sacrament.
DISTRIBUTE, v.t. — To administer, as justice; to dispense; to assign in due proportion. Distributing to the necessity of saints (Rom 12:13).
scriptures: Now when Jesus heard these things, he said unto him, Yet lackest thou one thing: sell all that thou hast, and distribute unto the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, follow me.
And laid them down at the apostles' feet: and distribution was made unto every man according as he had need.
Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality.
That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate;
corruption_summary: Distribution gets pulled between two errors—confiscation renamed charity, and hoarding defended with a verse—while Scripture's version is voluntary, accountable, need-based, and done by the church rather than outsourced.
corruption_paragraphs: One error reads Acts 4 as a policy platform and concludes that compulsory transfer is the Christian arrangement. The text will not carry it. The giving was voluntary—Peter tells Ananias the property was his and the proceeds were in his own power, which means his sin was the lie, not the withholding—and the distributing was done by the church, face to face, to people whose need was known. Compulsion cannot produce what Paul calls a cheerful giver, and distance cannot produce the accountability Acts describes.

The opposite error is more common in prosperous churches: a theology of stewardship that functions mainly to justify accumulation, with generosity redefined as whatever is left after the plan is fully funded. Paul's charge to the rich in 1 Timothy 6 does not tell them to divest; it tells them to be ready to distribute—a settled readiness of hand, not an annual gesture. And Christ's word to the young ruler is a permanent warning that for a particular man, at a particular moment, the command may be total, and refusing it is what walking away from Jesus looks like.
roots_summary: Greek diadidōmi, to give through or hand out, and koinōnikos, ready to share; Hebrew chalaq, to divide or apportion.
roots_lines: Greek diadidōmi (G1239) — to distribute, deal out, hand around; Christ's command to the rich ruler (Luke 11:22; 18:22; John 6:11; Acts 4:35).
Greek koinōnikos (G2843) — ready to share, sociable in giving; rendered willing to communicate in 1 Tim 6:18, from the same root as koinōnia, fellowship.
Hebrew chalaq (H2505) — to divide, apportion, share out; used of dividing the land by lot and of sharing spoil (Josh 18:2; 1 Sam 30:24; Prov 17:2).
usage: Distribution was made unto every man according as he had need—by need, not by equal shares.
Ready to distribute—a settled disposition of the hand, not an annual gesture.
Acts 4 is voluntary and accountable: the property was his own, and the church knew the need.

etymology: Old French norir, from Latin nutrire, to suckle, feed, rear—the root of nurse, nurture, and nutrition. To nourish is to feed a living thing toward growth, over time.
biblical_def: To nourish is to feed so as to sustain and grow, and Scripture uses it of bodies, households, churches and souls. God speaks of Israel as a father describing a raised child: I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me (Isa 1:2)—the tragedy is sharpened by the years of feeding that preceded the rebellion. Ruth's neighbors say of Obed that he shall be a nourisher of thine old age to Naomi, which is what covenant family does when the strength runs out at the far end of life. Paul's most weighted use is marital, and he argues from the body: no man ever yet hated his own flesh; but nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the church (Eph 5:29). A husband's duty toward his wife is set by two patterns at once—the automatic care every man gives his own body, and Christ's care of the church. Nourishing is therefore not romance and not provision only; it is the steady feeding of another life toward health. The pastoral form is Paul to Timothy: a good minister is one nourished up in the words of faith and of good doctrine (1 Tim 4:6). Note the passive—the minister is himself fed before he feeds anyone. Scripture also knows the counterfeit; James warns of men who have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter, feeding on the wages they withheld.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines NOURISH as to feed and cause to grow; to supply with nutriment; to support; to maintain by feeding; and figuratively, to encourage, foster, or promote growth in.
webster_full: NOURISH, v.t. — To feed and cause to grow; to supply a living being with matter which increases its bulk or supplies the waste occasioned by the vital functions.
NOURISH, v.t. — To support; to maintain by feeding. Also, to encourage; to foster; to cherish; as, to nourish a hope, or to nourish rebellion. I have nourished and brought up children (Isa 1:2).
scriptures: For no man ever yet hated his own flesh; but nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the church:
If thou put the brethren in remembrance of these things, thou shalt be a good minister of Jesus Christ, nourished up in the words of faith and of good doctrine, whereunto thou hast attained.
Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth: for the LORD hath spoken, I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me.
corruption_summary: Nourishment has been privatized as self-care and simultaneously cheapened into content—a man can feel well-fed on both and still be feeding no one, and be growing nothing that lasts.
corruption_paragraphs: The self-care vocabulary has annexed the language of feeding while removing its object. To nourish oneself is now a complete sentence, and the question of who else is being fed does not arise. Ephesians 5:29 uses self-nourishment as the assumed baseline—of course a man feeds his own body—and then makes it the measure of what he owes his wife. The instinct is not condemned; it is conscripted. A man who has learned to feed himself expertly and feeds no one else has taken the premise of the verse and refused its conclusion.

The second corruption is nutritional in the spiritual sense: volume mistaken for feeding. Clips, feeds, devotionals of a paragraph, sermons optimized for retention—a believer can consume religious material all day and remain unfed, because nourishing in Scripture is slow, repetitive, and aimed at growth rather than at stimulation. Paul's phrase is instructive: the minister is nourished up in the words of faith and of good doctrine, passive and over time. Nobody grows on snacks, and no one can feed a church out of an empty pantry.
roots_summary: Greek ektrephō, to nourish up or rear to maturity; Hebrew gadal, to make great or bring up—the verb of Isaiah's grieved fatherhood.
roots_lines: Greek ektrephō (G1625) — to nourish up, rear to maturity; used of a man's own flesh, of Christ and the church, and of fathers bringing up children (Eph 5:29; 6:4).
Greek entrephō (G1789) — to nourish in or train up in; nourished up in the words of faith (1 Tim 4:6).
Hebrew gadal (H1431) — to grow, become great, bring up; I have nourished and brought up children (Isa 1:2; 23:4; Dan 1:5).
usage: Nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the church—the husband's standard, set twice.
Nourished up in the words of faith—passive, and slow. The minister is fed before he feeds.
Isaiah 1:2 — God as the father who fed the children who then rebelled.

etymology: Latin satisfacere: satis (enough) + facere (to make)—to make enough. The theological term satisfaction, of a debt or of justice, comes from the same root, and the KJV holds both senses in view.
biblical_def: To satisfy is to make enough—to fill so that the want stops. Scripture's claim is that only God can do this for a soul, and that everything else which promises to is selling short weight. The Psalms state it directly: he satisfieth the longing soul, and filleth the hungry soul with goodness (Ps 107:9), and who satisfieth thy mouth with good things; so that thy youth is renewed like the eagle's (Ps 103:5). David's most piercing use is eschatological, and he is honest that the satisfaction is not yet: As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness (Ps 17:15). Note the tense. Full satisfaction waits for waking, which is why a Christian who feels a residual ache in the best of circumstances is not defective but accurately calibrated. Isaiah puts the market question to a people spending on the wrong goods: Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? (Isa 55:2). The indictment is not that they wanted satisfaction, but that they paid for a counterfeit. Ecclesiastes runs the experiment to its end—the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear with hearing—and the appetite outlasts every supply. Scripture therefore neither condemns desire nor promises its immediate end. It names the only source that is enough, and dates the full payment.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SATISFY as to gratify want or desire fully; to supply to the full extent; to feed to the full; and to pay in full—to answer or discharge a claim or debt.
webster_full: SATISFY, v.t. — To gratify wants, wishes or desires to the full extent; to supply possession or enjoyment till no more is desired. He satisfieth the longing soul (Ps 107:9).
SATISFY, v.t. — To pay to content; to discharge, as a claim or debt; to answer or discharge, as a legal demand. Hence SATISFACTION, the payment of a debt or the atonement for an offense.
scriptures: As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness.
For he satisfieth the longing soul, and filleth the hungry soul with goodness.

Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.
Who satisfieth thy mouth with good things; so that thy youth is renewed like the eagle's.
corruption_summary: An entire economy is now built on ensuring that satisfaction never arrives—appetite engineered to renew itself—while the older theological sense, satisfaction as a debt fully paid, has nearly vanished from ordinary speech.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern market does not sell satisfaction; it sells the approach to it. Feeds are built to prevent the stopping point, and a product that genuinely made a man content would be a commercial failure. Isaiah's question lands squarely on it: wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? The problem was never that Israel was hungry. The problem was the purchase. A culture with unprecedented supply and unprecedented restlessness is the exact condition the verse describes.

The second loss is doctrinal. Satisfaction once meant a debt paid in full, and the church used it of the atonement—Christ satisfying divine justice on behalf of sinners. Reduced to a customer-service word, it can no longer carry that weight, and the cross gets explained in vaguer terms. Keeping both senses keeps the logic intact: the God who satisfies the longing soul is the same God whose justice was satisfied, and Psalm 17:15 dates the believer's full portion—when I awake—which is honest about the ache that remains until then.
roots_summary: Hebrew saba, to be sated or have enough; Greek chortazō, to feed until full—the verb of the fed multitudes and of the beatitude on hunger for righteousness.
roots_lines: Hebrew saba (H7646) — to be satisfied, sated, have enough; used of food, of riches that fail to satisfy, and of the soul satisfied in God (Ps 17:15; 103:5; Prov 27:20; Eccl 5:10).
Hebrew ravah (H7301) — to be saturated, drink one's fill; the soul watered like a garden (Ps 36:8; Jer 31:14).
Greek chortazō (G5526) — to feed, fill, satisfy with food; used of the fed multitudes and of those who hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled (Matt 5:6; 14:20; Phil 4:12).
usage: I shall be satisfied, when I awake—the tense is future, and the honesty is deliberate.
Your labour for that which satisfieth not—the sin is the purchase, not the hunger.
Satisfaction also means a debt paid in full — the sense the atonement requires.

etymology: Old French devis, from Latin dividere, to divide—a thing distinguished, hence a design, plan, or emblem. In the KJV a device is a scheme conceived in the heart, not a tool held in the hand.
biblical_def: In the KJV a device is a plan, scheme or invention formed in the heart, and the word is morally loaded by whoever is doing the devising. Of men: There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand (Prov 19:21)—a verse that concedes the ingenuity and then quietly outranks it. Of the crafty specifically: He disappointeth the devices of the crafty, so that their hands cannot perform their enterprise (Job 5:12), matched by the psalmist's national version, the LORD bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought: he maketh the devices of the people of none effect (Ps 33:10). Of Satan: Paul says the church forgives so that Satan gains no advantage, for we are not ignorant of his devices (2 Cor 2:11)—which assumes both that the enemy works by patterned schemes and that a church can learn them. The word also carries a neutral or good sense: Bezaleel is filled with the Spirit to devise cunning works for the tabernacle, and Isaiah says the liberal man deviseth liberal things. So devising itself is a faculty of the image-bearer. What Scripture keeps insisting is that the human heart is a device factory running continuously—Genesis 6:5 says every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually—and that God's counsel stands over the entire output.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DEVICE as that which is formed by design; a contrivance; an invention; a scheme formed, especially an evil one; and also an emblem or heraldic figure with a motto.
webster_full: DEVICE, n. — That which is formed by design, or invented; scheme; artificial contrivance; stratagem; project. They imagined a mischievous device (Ps 21:11).
DEVICE, n. — An emblem painted or engraved, with a motto or legend, as on a shield. Also, invention; genius; faculty of devising.
scriptures: Lest Satan should get an advantage of us: for we are not ignorant of his devices.
He disappointeth the devices of the crafty, so that their hands cannot perform their enterprise.
The LORD bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought: he maketh the devices of the people of none effect.
There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand.
corruption_summary: Device now names a machine, so the KJV's meaning inverts on contact: readers picture hardware where Scripture means a scheme of the heart, and the moral weight moves from the schemer to the gadget.
corruption_paragraphs: The semantic drift is complete—a device is a phone, a tablet, a piece of hardware—and the drift does theological damage. When 2 Corinthians 2:11 says we are not ignorant of Satan's devices, it means his patterned schemes, several of which Paul names elsewhere: unforgiveness left to fester, ignorance of the gospel, an angel of light, accusation. Read as machinery, the verse becomes a warning about screens and the actual warning is lost.

There is a second and more convenient corruption: locating evil in the tools. Blaming the device is comfortable because devices can be regulated, upgraded, or set aside, whereas Proverbs locates the devices in the heart and Genesis 6:5 says the factory never shuts down. Technology genuinely shapes and amplifies—that much is true—but Scripture keeps the accounting straight. The instrument is not the schemer. And the same faculty that devises mischief is the one the Spirit filled in Bezaleel to devise cunning work for the tabernacle, which means the answer to bad devising is not the abolition of ingenuity but its consecration.
roots_summary: Hebrew machashabah, a thought, plan or device, from the accounting verb chashab; Greek noēma, a thought or scheme of the mind.
