roots_lines: Hebrew machashabah (H4284) — a thought, plan, invention, device; used of men's schemes, of Bezaleel's cunning works, and of God's own thoughts toward His people (Gen 6:5; Exod 31:4; Jer 29:11).
Hebrew mezimmah (H4209) — a plan, purpose, or wicked device; also discretion in a good sense (Prov 1:4; 12:2; Jer 11:15).
Greek noēma (G3540) — a thought, purpose, design of the mind; we are not ignorant of his devices (2 Cor 2:11; 4:4; 10:5; 11:3).
usage: We are not ignorant of his devices—schemes of an enemy, not hardware.
Many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand.
The same devising faculty filled Bezaleel for the tabernacle; ingenuity is to be consecrated, not abolished.

etymology: Latin pertinere: per- (through, thoroughly) + tenere (to hold)—to hold through, to belong to. The KJV uses it as a word of jurisdiction: what belongs to whom, and therefore who may handle it.
biblical_def: Pertain is the KJV's word for belonging, and its work is to mark jurisdiction—this belongs here and not there. Hebrews describes the priesthood in exactly these terms: every high priest taken from among men is ordained for men in things pertaining to God, that he may offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins (Heb 5:1). There is a category of things that pertain to God, and men do not walk into it uncommissioned; a priest is ordained for that jurisdiction. Peter's promise runs the other direction: God's divine power hath given unto us all things that pertain unto life and godliness, through the knowledge of him (2 Pet 1:3)—everything belonging to that domain has already been supplied, which forecloses the search for a missing key. Paul, boasting carefully, restricts his glorying to those things which pertain to God (Rom 15:17). The New Testament also uses the verb to sort the ordinary from the sacred: Paul tells the Corinthians that if they have judgments of things pertaining to this life, they should set the least esteemed in the church to judge them rather than dragging brothers before pagan courts (1 Cor 6:3-4)—a startling ranking, since saints who will judge angels can certainly handle a property dispute. The consistent effect of the word is to draw lines: some things pertain to God, some to Caesar, some to the elders, some to the marriage bed alone.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PERTAIN as to belong; to be the property, right or duty of; and to relate to, or concern—a word of belonging and of jurisdiction.
webster_full: PERTAIN, v.i. — To belong; to be the property, right or duty of. Things pertaining to God (Heb 5:1).
PERTAIN, v.i. — To have relation to; to concern; to regard. Hence PERTINENT, that which belongs to the matter in hand.
scriptures: According as his divine power hath given unto us all things that pertain unto life and godliness, through the knowledge of him that hath called us to glory and virtue:
For every high priest taken from among men is ordained for men in things pertaining to God, that he may offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins:
I have therefore whereof I may glory through Jesus Christ in those things which pertain to God.
corruption_summary: The age recognizes no jurisdictions—every matter is everyone's to weigh in on, and every private thing is publishable—so the biblical habit of asking what pertains to whom has no place left to stand.
corruption_paragraphs: Two collapses run at once. Outward: nothing is anyone else's business anymore in the sense of being off-limits, so private griefs, marriages, and family conflicts are narrated publicly and adjudicated by strangers who have no standing in the matter. Inward: nothing is anyone else's business in the sense of accountability, so a man's conduct is held to pertain to him alone and no elder, father or friend may speak to it. Both are failures to ask the biblical question, which is not whether a matter is interesting but to whom it belongs.

Scripture's jurisdictions are specific and worth naming. Some things pertain to God and require an ordained approach, which is Hebrews 5:1. Some pertain to the civil magistrate, which is Romans 13. Some pertain to the church's own courts—Paul is indignant that Christians take internal disputes to outsiders when saints who will judge angels are sitting right there. Some pertain to the marriage bed and to no one else. And per 2 Peter 1:3, everything pertaining to life and godliness has already been given, which means the Christian's problem is almost never a missing resource in his own jurisdiction.
roots_summary: Greek pros with the accusative, things toward God; and anēkō, to be fitting or proper to—what belongs in a given domain.
roots_lines: Greek ta pros ton theon — literally the things toward God; the standard phrase rendered things pertaining to God in the priestly texts (Rom 15:17; Heb 2:17; 5:1).
Greek anēkō (G433) — to be fitting, proper, becoming; what pertains to a saint's conduct (Eph 5:4; Col 3:18; Phm 1:8).
Greek biotikos (G982) — pertaining to this life, everyday; the disputes Paul says the church can settle among itself (Luke 21:34; 1 Cor 6:3-4).
usage: Things pertaining to God—a jurisdiction a man does not enter uncommissioned.
All things that pertain unto life and godliness have already been given.
1 Corinthians 6 — matters pertaining to this life belong in the church, not in a pagan court.

etymology: Old French medler, a variant of mesler, to mix, from Latin miscere—the root of mix and miscellaneous. To meddle is to mix oneself into what one was not mixed into.
biblical_def: To meddle is to mix yourself into a matter that is not yours, and Proverbs treats it as a mark of folly rather than of zeal. The central image is unforgettable: He that passeth by, and meddleth with strife belonging not to him, is like one that taketh a dog by the ears (Prov 26:17)—a man who was merely walking past, who reaches into a fight he had no part in, and who now cannot let go without being bitten. Proverbs contrasts it with honor: It is an honour for a man to cease from strife: but every fool will be meddling (Prov 20:3). Ceasing is the honorable move; the fool cannot leave it alone. There is also a political form: My son, fear thou the LORD and the king: and meddle not with them that are given to change (Prov 24:21)—keep clear of the perpetually agitated, the men whose settled posture is overthrow. And there is a sober historical example. Josiah, a genuinely good king, rides out against Pharaoh Necho, who sends word, What have I to do with thee, thou king of Judah? ... forbear thee from meddling with God, who is with me, that he destroy thee not (2 Chr 35:21). Josiah meddles anyway and dies of it. That is the warning Proverbs is making practical: meddling is not always the vice of a bad man. It is often the last mistake of a good one who could not stay out of a quarrel God had not assigned him.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MEDDLE as to have to do with; to interpose or interfere officiously; to take part in the concerns of others which do not belong to one, and where one has no business.
webster_full: MEDDLE, v.i. — To have to do; to take part; to interpose or interfere. Usually followed by with.
MEDDLE, v.i. — To interpose or interfere officiously; to act in the concerns of others without being invited or having a right. Every fool will be meddling (Prov 20:3).
scriptures: It is an honour for a man to cease from strife: but every fool will be meddling.
He that passeth by, and meddleth with strife belonging not to him, is like one that taketh a dog by the ears.
My son, fear thou the LORD and the king: and meddle not with them that are given to change:
corruption_summary: The internet turned meddling into a civic duty—every distant quarrel presented as a matter requiring your position—so that a man now spends his attention on fights he cannot affect and neglects the field actually assigned to him.
corruption_paragraphs: The economics are simple: platforms profit from engagement, and nothing engages like a quarrel. So a man is served, all day, strife belonging not to him—other people's marriages, other cities' politics, other churches' scandals—each framed as something on which silence would be complicity. Proverbs 26:17 describes exactly this posture, and the trap in it: the passer-by grabs the ears, and now letting go costs blood. Anyone who has tried to exit a public argument knows the verse is literal.

The needful distinction is between meddling and duty. Scripture commands intervention in specific places: deliver those drawn unto death, rebuke a brother, defend the fatherless and the widow, restore a man overtaken in a fault. Those are assigned fields, and the assignment usually comes with proximity—a brother, a neighbor, a household, a flock. Meddling is what happens when a man skips the assigned field for the unassigned one, and the tell is that meddling costs him nothing but attention and gratifies him immediately, whereas the strife that actually belongs to him is close, slow, and thankless.
roots_summary: Hebrew garah, to stir up strife, and arab, to mix oneself in—the two ways a man gets into a quarrel that was not his.
roots_lines: Hebrew arab (H6148) — to mix, mingle, give oneself as a pledge; hence to intermeddle in another's affairs (Prov 14:10; 20:19; 24:21).
Hebrew garah (H1624) — to stir up, provoke, engage in strife; used of meddling in a quarrel and of provoking a war (Deut 2:5; Prov 15:18; 28:4; 2 Chr 35:21).
Hebrew galah (H1540) — to uncover, reveal; the companion sin of Prov 20:19, the talebearer who reveals secrets, with whom one is told not to meddle.
usage: Like one that taketh a dog by the ears—grabbing is easy; letting go costs blood.
It is an honour for a man to cease from strife—ceasing is the honorable move.
Josiah meddled with a quarrel God had not assigned him and died of it (2 Chr 35:21).

etymology: From rob, Old French rober, of Germanic origin, related to reave and bereave—to strip or plunder. A robber differs from a thief in Scripture and in Webster: the thief takes by stealth, the robber by force.
biblical_def: A robber takes by violence and openly, where a thief takes by stealth. Christ uses both words in one sentence at the sheepfold: He that entereth not by the door into the sheepfold, but climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber (John 10:1)—and He is describing religious leaders, not highwaymen. The men who came before Him claiming the flock are called robbers because they took what was not theirs, by force and by fraud, from people who could not resist. The same charge lands on the temple trade: My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves (Matt 21:13), the phrase drawn from Jeremiah, where the sanctuary has become the place robbers retreat to between jobs. God announces His own hatred of the pious version: I the LORD love judgment, I hate robbery for burnt offering (Isa 61:8)—stolen goods laid on the altar are not worship but an aggravation of the theft. Malachi presses the charge to its most audacious form: Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings (Mal 3:8)—withholding is classified as robbery, and the withholders are genuinely puzzled, which is the most instructive detail in the passage. The Good Samaritan's road supplies the ordinary sense, and Barabbas, released in Christ's place, is a robber by trade.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ROBBER as one that robs; one who takes goods or money from another by force or by putting him in fear—distinguishing robbery from theft, which is done secretly.
webster_full: ROBBER, n. — One that robs; in law, one that takes goods or money from the person of another by force or menaces, and with a felonious intent.
ROB, v.t. — To take from another by force or menaces; to plunder; to strip unlawfully. Distinguished from theft, which is a secret taking. Will a man rob God? (Mal 3:8).
scriptures: Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that entereth not by the door into the sheepfold, but climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber.
And said unto them, It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves.
For I the LORD love judgment, I hate robbery for burnt offering; and I will direct their work in truth, and I will make an everlasting covenant with them.
Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings.
corruption_summary: Robbery is now recognized only when a stranger uses a weapon—so systems that strip people by force of law or of process, and religious enterprises that take from the flock, escape a word Scripture aims squarely at both.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture's robbers are frequently respectable. John 10 aims the word at shepherds who climbed into the fold another way; Matthew 21 aims it at a trade operating inside the temple with the chief priests' blessing; Isaiah 61 aims it at worshippers bringing stolen goods to the altar. None of these would have described himself as a robber. The modern narrowing—robbery as an armed stranger—lets every institutional and religious form of the sin pass unnamed, which is precisely the form Scripture spends most of its energy on.

Malachi supplies the sharpest and most personal test, and the tone matters. Wherein have we robbed thee? is asked in genuine bewilderment by people who considered themselves worshippers, and the answer is withholding—in tithes and offerings. That establishes a category the modern conscience resists: a man can rob by keeping. The category also cuts against the profiteering it is often quoted to fund. A ministry that uses Malachi 3 to extract money it then spends on itself has become the den of Matthew 21, and Isaiah's line covers the case—God hates robbery for burnt offering, whichever direction it flows.
roots_summary: Hebrew gazal, to seize or tear away by violence, and qaba, to rob—Malachi's verb; Greek lēstēs, a bandit, the word for Barabbas and for the two crucified beside Christ.
roots_lines: Hebrew gazal (H1497) — to tear away, seize, rob by violence; forbidden against the poor and the hired man (Lev 19:13; Prov 22:22; Isa 61:8).
Hebrew qaba (H6906) — to rob or defraud; the verb of Malachi 3:8-9, will a man rob God?
Greek lēstēs (G3027) — a robber, bandit, one who plunders openly; used of Barabbas, of the two crucified with Christ, and of the den of thieves (Matt 21:13; 27:38; Luke 10:30; John 10:1; 18:40).
usage: A thief and a robber—aimed at false shepherds, not highwaymen.
I hate robbery for burnt offering—stolen goods on the altar aggravate the theft.
Wherein have we robbed thee?—a man can rob by keeping, and not notice.

etymology: Plain English rendering Hebrew yamin and Greek dexia, both meaning the right side. In the ancient world the right hand was the hand of strength, of oath-taking, of blessing, and of the place of honor beside a king.
biblical_def: Right hand is one of Scripture's heaviest phrases, and it carries three loads. First, power: Thy right hand, O LORD, is become glorious in power: thy right hand, O LORD, hath dashed in pieces the enemy (Exod 15:6)—the LORD's right hand is His acting strength in history. Second, favor and joy: at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore (Ps 16:11), and the sheep are set on the right hand in the judgment. Third, and decisively, the enthronement of the Son. Psalm 110 opens with a line the New Testament quotes more than any other Old Testament verse: The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool (Ps 110:1). Christ applies it to Himself before the Sanhedrin; Peter preaches it at Pentecost; Hebrews organizes its entire argument around it—the priest who sat down, because the work was finished. Mark records the ascension in the same terms: he was received up into heaven, and sat on the right hand of God (Mark 16:19). Stephen sees the one exception to the sitting: Jesus standing on the right hand of God (Acts 7:55), the enthroned Lord risen to His feet for a dying martyr. The right hand is therefore not a location in space but a statement of rank, authority and acceptance—which is why the Creed says it and why it matters that a man in our nature is there.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 notes that the right hand denotes the place of honor and of power—the side of dignity and strength—and that to be at one's right hand is to hold the position of favor and authority.
webster_full: RIGHT HAND — The hand opposite to the left; among all nations, the hand of strength and of honor. To sit at the right hand of a prince is to occupy the place of highest dignity and authority.
In Scripture, the right hand of God denotes his power and his favor; and Christ's session at the right hand of the Father denotes his exaltation, dominion, and finished priestly work.
scriptures: The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool.
So then after the Lord had spoken unto them, he was received up into heaven, and sat on the right hand of God.
But he, being full of the Holy Ghost, looked up stedfastly into heaven, and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God,
Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.
corruption_summary: Where the phrase survives at all it means a useful subordinate—someone's right-hand man—which loses both the enthronement it names in Scripture and the finished work signaled by the fact that the Priest sat down.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern usage keeps a shadow of the honor sense: a right-hand man is a trusted lieutenant. Scripture's meaning is enthronement, not assistance. Psalm 110:1 has a Lord seated beside the LORD, sharing the throne, with enemies being made a footstool in the interval—which is why the verse is the New Testament's favorite proof of Christ's deity and present reign. Reduced to a metaphor for a capable deputy, the phrase can no longer do that work.

The detail most often lost is the posture. Hebrews contrasts the priests who standeth daily ministering, whose work is never finished, with the one who after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God. The sitting is the argument: no further offering is needed or possible. And Stephen's vision is the deliberate exception that proves it—the seated Lord standing for a servant being stoned. Both postures preach, and a reader who hears only right-hand man will catch neither.
roots_summary: Hebrew yamin, the right hand or south side, the hand of strength and oath; Greek dexios, right—the side of honor at a throne.
roots_lines: Hebrew yamin (H3225) — the right hand or side; the hand of power, of blessing, and of the oath (Exod 15:6; Ps 16:11; 110:1; Isa 41:10).
Greek dexios (G1188) — right, of the right side; used of Christ's session, of the sheep in the judgment, and of the right hand of fellowship (Matt 25:33; Mark 16:19; Acts 7:55; Gal 2:9).
Greek kathizō (G2523) — to sit down, be seated; the verb whose perfect force carries the argument of Hebrews, the priest who sat (Heb 1:3; 8:1; 10:12; 12:2).
usage: Sit thou at my right hand—the Old Testament verse the New Testament quotes most.
The Priest sat down; the work is finished. Levitical priests never sat.
Stephen sees Him standing—the enthroned Lord on His feet for a dying martyr.

etymology: English rendering of Greek archiereis, plural of archiereus—arch- (chief) + hiereus (priest). The plural is significant: Israel's law provided one high priest, yet the Gospels record a standing body of them.
biblical_def: The chief priests are the ruling priestly aristocracy of Jerusalem in the Gospels and Acts—the serving high priest, former high priests still holding influence, and the heads of the priestly families, largely Sadducean and tied to the temple's administration and revenue. They appear almost exclusively as an acting body, and almost always in opposition. They convene the council: Then gathered the chief priests and the Pharisees a council, and said, What do we? for this man doeth many miracles (John 11:47)—the miracles are conceded, and the concern is institutional. They assemble at Caiaphas's palace to plot (Matt 26:3). They work the crowd: the chief priests and elders persuaded the multitude that they should ask Barabbas, and destroy Jesus (Matt 27:20). And their authority continues after the resurrection, since Saul travels to Damascus with warrants from them (Acts 9:14). The plural itself tells part of the story. The law appointed one high priest for life; by the first century Rome appointed and deposed them, which produced a bench of men who had held the office and a family interest in keeping the arrangement stable. That is the setting of the most self-aware line in the Passion—Caiaphas reasoning that it is expedient that one man die for the people. The office God established for mediation had become a position to protect, and it was defended against the very Priest it prefigured.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines the CHIEF PRIEST as the high priest, the principal of the priestly order; in the New Testament the plural denotes the heads of the twenty-four courses together with those who had borne the high priesthood.
webster_full: CHIEF PRIEST — The high priest; the principal officer of the Levitical order, who alone entered the holy of holies once a year with blood.

CHIEF PRIESTS, n. pl. — In the New Testament, the ruling body of the priesthood at Jerusalem: the acting high priest, those who had held the office, and the heads of the priestly courses. The chief priests and elders persuaded the multitude (Matt 27:20).
scriptures: Then assembled together the chief priests, and the scribes, and the elders of the people, unto the palace of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas,
Then gathered the chief priests and the Pharisees a council, and said, What do we? for this man doeth many miracles.
But the chief priests and elders persuaded the multitude that they should ask Barabbas, and destroy Jesus.
And here he hath authority from the chief priests to bind all that call on thy name.
corruption_summary: The phrase is usually flattened into generic religious villains, which lets every reader place himself among the persecuted—where the text's actual warning is aimed at office-holders defending an institution against God's own work in it.
corruption_paragraphs: Read as stock antagonists, the chief priests carry no warning for anyone. Read accurately, they are men holding legitimate, God-established office, who conceded the miracles and opposed Him anyway because of what His ministry would cost the institution. John 11:47-48 states the reasoning in the open: if we let him alone, all will believe, and the Romans will take away our place and nation. That is not the logic of unbelief but of institutional preservation, and it is available to any board, elder-body or ministry with something to protect.

A second and uglier corruption is the use of these texts to indict a people rather than an office. The Gospels are careful in a way their readers often are not: the crowd had to be persuaded (Matt 27:20), the priests feared the people, and thousands of Jerusalem Jews—including, Acts records, a great company of the priests—believed shortly afterward. The indictment falls on a specific ruling body in a specific alliance with Rome, not on a nation. The permanent lesson is what happens when a mediating office becomes a position to defend, and Hebrews answers it by naming a High Priest who cannot be deposed and needs nothing protected.
roots_summary: Greek archiereus, chief priest or high priest—used of Caiaphas and his colleagues, and, in Hebrews, of Christ Himself.
roots_lines: Greek archiereus (G749) — chief priest, high priest; in the plural the ruling priestly body, in the singular both Caiaphas and Christ (Matt 26:3; John 11:47; Heb 4:14-15).
Greek hiereus (G2409) — a priest, one who offers sacrifice; the ordinary priests, and the believers made priests unto God (Luke 1:5; Rev 1:6).
Greek synedrion (G4892) — the council, Sanhedrin; the body the chief priests convened against Christ and later against the apostles (Matt 26:59; John 11:47; Acts 5:21).
usage: What do we? for this man doeth many miracles—the miracles conceded, the institution defended.
The crowd had to be persuaded; the indictment falls on a ruling body, not a people.
A God-given office turned into a position to protect — and defended against the true Priest.
